title: Why a late-dropping Karol G hit single could be the front-runner for inaugural Best Latin Song Grammy - Gold Derby

				We use vendors that may also process your information to help provide our services. Karol G is riding high. She became the first Latina artist to headline Coachella back in April, her seven Latin Grammy nominations last week tied Rosalía, Jorge Drexler, and Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso for the most among artists, and her highly anticipated album No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto remains in the Top 20 of the Billboard charts — firmly establishing the Colombian superstar in the cultural conversation and positioning her for a historical Grammy run. She dropped No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto on Aug. 7, and the album became an instant hit. It debuted at No. 8 on the Billboard 200 and currently sits at No. 11. While the album was expected to achieve widespread success, following the performances of previous projects Tropicoqueta and Mañana Será Bonito, what was less predictable was the massive response to one particular track: "Bby Wow." The party anthem did not receive the same level of promotion as other songs on the album. It was not released as a single and does not have an official music video, unlike the song "Still," and didn't have as much prerelease buzz as her collaborations with globally popular artists, notably "Ahí" with Drake, "Still" with Bruno Mars, and "Después de Ti" with Greg González of Sleeping With Sirens. While those collabs gained visibility and secured strong chart positions, none has matched the success of "Bby Wow." So far, the song has earned more than 161 million streams on Spotify, remained at No. 1 on Spotify Global since Aug. 28, and recently reached the Top 10 of the Billboard Hot 100. It also surpassed Ella Langley's ubiquitous "Choosin’ Texas" on the U.S. Apple Music chart and reached No. 1 on the Billboard Global 200. The collaboration with Spanish singers Judeline and Rusowsky demonstrates that when a song connects with an audience, the artists’ existing levels of fame do not necessarily determine its impact. The track has also benefited Judeline and Rusowsky, giving the emerging artists greater visibility and expanding their reach in the English-language music industry. Karol G has continued to demonstrate an ability to recognize new talent, giving rising artists a platform and highlighting her commitment to creating opportunities for new voices in music. With all of that in mind, "Bby Wow" has emerged as the potential front-runner for the Grammys’ new Best Latin Song category, with one big caveat. Gold Derby has been unable to confirm whether Karol G’s team submitted the track before the Recording Academy’s deadline. Although the album was released Aug. 7, the song didn't really achieve its breakthrough until the week of Aug. 28, which was the final day for artists to enter music for Grammy consideration. That means there's a chance her team might hold off on submitting the track until the next awards cycle, which could prove challenging, since it relies on voters having long memories. If "Bby Wow" isn't in contention this year, Karol G's team could instead prioritize her Latin Grammy-nominated hit "Coleccionando Heridas" from Tropicoqueta (as Gold Derby predicted back in July) or the new album’s lead single, "Matadora." In any case, Karol G will definitely be on the shortlist of viable artists for Best Latin Song, alongside fellow Latin Grammy nominees Rosalía, Silvana Estrada, and Jorge Drexler. title: Isaiah Rodgers Named NFC Special Teams Player of the Week for Week 2 - Minnesota Vikings
content: EAGAN, Minn. — Isaiah Rodgers was involved in two game-defining plays. On the first Sunday in Chicago, he dove on a fumble at the goal line, forced by Jalen Redmond, that kept the Bears out of the end zone in the third quarter, then did the "Hot Dog, Hot Dog, Hot Diggity Dog" dance to fulfill a promise to his son. On the second, he zoomed off the edge with six-and-a-half minutes left and rejected a 23-yard field goal attempt by Cairo Santos. The play preserved a 6-3 lead on the way to Minnesota's 9-3 win. It also earned Rodgers NFC Special Teams Player of the Week honors, the NFL announced Wednesday. The cornerback won his first career POTW accolade 364 days ago when he was named the NFC Defensive Player of the Week for his performance of epic proportions in a 2025 Week 3 blowout of Cincinnati. In this instance, he made a brilliant impact on defense, recovering the fumble that turned the tide amidst the slosh at Soldier Field — but his block sent him over the top. In response, Minnesota's offense marched 11 plays, tying its longest possession (by number of plays) of the game and returned the ball after another Will Reichard field goal with 1:09 on the clock. Vikings Special Teams Coordinator Matt Daniels gave his thoughts on the moment Tuesday and listed a number of impressive aspects: Rodgers' ability to eliminate the space between him and the holder; his skill at dodging or knocking down the arm of the "wing" on the end of the line of scrimmage (rookie tight end Sam Roush on this occasion); his preparation and expertise of the opponent's operation; and, of course, his ball get-off in slippery conditions. "Everyone knows that this guy is probably one of the fastest guys in the NFL, but his acceleration to get off of the football and be able to bend," Daniels said. "His ability to slip Roush's hand that got thrown out and be able to bend and be able to take it off the foot — [it] says a lot about the type of athlete that he is, and on plays like that we say it all the time that 'Great plays are made from great effort,' and it was just unbelievable effort by him." Rodgers has done this before for the Purple. He blocked a 30-yard try by Pittsburgh's Chris Boswell, who is close to automatic on kicks under 40 yards in his career (94.6%) during the Ireland game last season. And Rodgers has stated his plans to do it again — and again. "He's already kind of put it out in the air that he's going to take three; he's going to take three off the foot this year," Daniels shared that Rodgers expressed that intention right before the game vs. Green Bay. "That's surely enough the first thing he said when he came to the sidelines [this Sunday], 'That's one Hat, that's one. I got two more to go this year,' so we're off to a good start there." Rodgers got a hand on Santos' 50-yarder on Chicago's opening drive, as well. View game action photos from the Vikings Week 2 game vs. the Bears at Soldier Field. "His pinky wasn't big enough, I guess, to deflect it enough," Daniels quipped. But his near block early on likely affected Chicago's failure to launch later. The sight of Rodgers lined up in a track stance and threatening his speed, at this point, is a warning. "Absolutely," Daniels said opposing kickers are thinking about a possible block. "100%." On Daniels' watch, the Vikings have done a fabulous job of instilling that fear. While opponents have attempted the second-most field goals against Minnesota since 2022 (160), they've converted only 83.1%. That's the 10th lowest hit rate in the NFL in that span, following the Browns (79.1%), Bears (79.3%), 49ers (81.1%), Buccaneers (81.3%), Giants (81.5%), Raiders (82%), Seahawks (82.7%), Patriots (82.9%) and Chargers (83%). Santos has suffered the second-most blocked field goals (five) during that timeframe, by the way. Who has more? title: LEGO x Nike Air Force 1 Low GS “Outer Space”: the space mission for kids this Holiday 2026 - selecta bisso
content: Nike and LEGO are extending their iconic collaboration by pushing the streetwear universe to the far reaches of space. Scheduled for release in Holiday 2026, the new LEGO x Nike Air Force 1 Low GS “Outer Space” is designed for children and promises a playful and visually engaging experience that echoes LEGO’s space-themed history. Designed as an homage to exploration, this Air Force 1 Low GS features a predominantly white upper that perfectly complements the space theme. The upper is accented with visible black stitching and gray toggle laces, adding a technical and futuristic touch. Graphic overlays and details, including striped pull tabs on the tongue and heel, reinforce the astronaut aesthetic while remaining true to Nike's identity. One of the most striking elements is the Swoosh, designed as a rocket orbiting a yellow planet. A subtle yet powerful nod to the space imagery that has accompanied space missions since LEGO's beginnings in the 1970s. Hidden behind the tongue is a small LEGO minifigure that resembles a robotic space companion or perhaps an explorer penguin—a playful detail typical of collaborations between the two brands. The connection between LEGO and space is nothing new. LEGO incorporated the space theme into its product lines as early as 1978 with sets focused on astronauts and lunar exploration, a universe that later expanded to include robots, aliens, and futuristic vehicles. More recently, LEGO and Nike have explored this theme through collaborative projects, such as a 1,093-piece set depicting an Air Force 1 launched to the moon, accompanied by a LEGO spaceman sporting the Nike swoosh—a clear indication of the two brands' shared vision of space. The LEGO x Nike Air Force 1 Low GS “Outer Space” will retail for $120 and will be available starting November 24, 2026, on Nike.com and at select retailers. This limited edition, exclusively for kids, is part of a broader strategy to renew young consumers' interest in  sneakers while reintroducing the spirit of adventure and discovery symbolized by space. title: Nike Air Force 1 Low GS "5 Rings" Honors Kobe's Championship Legacy - KicksUnderCost
content: Nike is channeling Kobe Bryant's championship pedigree into a youth-focused Air Force 1 Low that threads his five NBA titles into its construction. The "5 Rings" edition marries Lakers iconography with intimate design details that reward closer inspection, releasing October 1, 2026. The execution here balances restraint with symbol. Black dominates the upper—a canvas that lets the complementary yellows and light blues speak without overwhelming the silhouette. Yellow Swooshes and matching heel tabs provide the primary color intervention, a direct nod to the Lakers' storied palette. The Air Force 1 Low's familiar structure remains intact; this isn't a radical reimagining, but rather a thoughtful layering of meaning onto an already-iconic form. Kobe's presence appears methodically throughout. Branded elements land on the tongue and heel, establishing visual hierarchy without noise. The rear heel caps carry numerical weight—"8" on one side, "24" on the other, the two jersey numbers that defined his career arc with Los Angeles. Lace dubraes read "MAMBA" and "FOREVER," references that connect directly to Kobe's personal mythology without divorcing the shoe from its core silhouette. The real narrative lives where most won't immediately look. Midsole graphics render in black, yellow, and light blue in a deliberately rough, painted aesthetic that contrasts the shoe's clean construction. That same treatment extends to the outsole. But the insoles are where the championship concept crystallizes: one features five championship rings printed across the interior, while the other visualizes a hand adorned with all five. It's economical storytelling—the kind of hidden detail that separates collaborative depth from surface-level branding. The Air Force 1 Low continues its role as Nike's most versatile canvas for athlete storytelling. From its foundational status in basketball culture to its ubiquity in contemporary streetwear, the silhouette absorbs narrative without demanding design gymnastics. Kobe-focused offerings on the Air Force 1 have become periodic touchstones—this youth-geared interpretation (GS sizing) ensures accessibility across age groups while maintaining the same design language. The Lakers color story remains potent across Nike's catalog, carrying historical weight that transcends single-player associations. Yet here it's specifically tethered to Kobe's two-decade tenure, making the yellow and black selection feel earned rather than generic. The Kobe Bryant x Nike Air Force 1 Low GS "5 Rings" arrives October 1, 2026. This timing positions it as a fall release, aligning with the broader Nike calendar. The GS sizing—kids' and youth proportions—signals Nike's intentional outreach to younger collectors and fans building their own sneaker literacy through athlete-focused offerings. title: Can AI Investment Drive S&P 500 Earnings Even Higher? - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. The recent strength of S&P 500 earnings has raised concerns among some investors that stocks are in an “earnings bubble,” according to Goldman Sachs Research. Our strategists expect the boost to earnings from investment in artificial intelligence (AI) to gradually fade, making productivity gains from AI increasingly important for stock profitability. Recent earnings growth has been “extraordinary,” writes Ben Snider, chief US equity strategist at Goldman Sachs Research, in a report. S&P 500 earnings per share (EPS) grew 51% in the second quarter (year over year) and 26% during the past four quarters. By comparison, the S&P 500’s four-quarter growth in EPS has averaged 7% during the past 30 years. Earnings have also pulled ahead of their historical relationship with US economic growth. “Our base case is for S&P 500 earnings growth to decelerate, not collapse, in coming years,” says Snider. “Because equity prices have failed to keep pace with surging earnings, near-term valuations show no hint of a bubble,” Snider writes. The forward price-to-earnings ratio has fallen from 23 times a year ago to 19 times today, matching its 10-year average. That said, “even an 'average' multiple may be expensive if current earnings are unsustainable,” he adds. The cyclically adjusted P/E ratio, which uses the trailing 10 years of earnings, has climbed to one of the highest readings on record. It falls short of the 1999-2000 peak but exceeds the level reached in 2021. Goldman Sachs Research forecasts the S&P 500 will rise to 8,700 over 12 months, up from 7,764 on September 21. Our strategists’ outlook implies a P/E multiple on consensus forward EPS that remains close to the current level of 19 times. Snider expects investors to remain uncertain in the coming quarters about AI’s impact on long-term profits, making a dramatic increase in valuations unlikely. S&P 500 EPS are forecast to grow about 11% in both 2027 (to $415) and 2028 ($460). Earnings are expected to be driven by solid GDP growth and a fading tailwind from AI investment that gradually transitions into a growing boost from AI productivity. “Energy prices and interest rates create near-term macro risks around these forecasts, but the impact of AI is the biggest long-term question for corporate earnings,” Snider writes. Almost half of S&P 500 growth in EPS in 2026 comes from AI investment, according to Goldman Sachs Research. The largest US hyperscaler companies are on track to spend $800 billion on capital expenditures this year, an increase of 94% over 2025. That money is flowing through the earnings of chipmakers, tech hardware suppliers, industrial firms, and utilities, Snider says. There are second-order effects too. The boom has lifted capital markets activity and supported consumer spending through rising household wealth. However, both consensus and Goldman Sachs Research analyst forecasts show hyperscaler capex growing at a slower rate in coming years. In the meantime, the hyperscalers’ equipment carries depreciation charges that keep climbing as spending growth slows. This will further dampen the boost of AI investment spending to S&P 500 earnings growth. “Hyperscaler capex has consistently surprised relative to consensus estimates during the last few years, and the potential for additional surprises going forward creates a wide range of potential S&P 500 earnings outcomes,” Snider writes. Goldman Sachs Research’s equity analysts expect $1.2 trillion of hyperscaler capex in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028. A surprise of $250 billion in either direction next year would move S&P 500 earnings growth by roughly 6 percentage points in the same direction, according to Goldman Sachs Research. Strong demand and tight supply have boosted semiconductor prices and gross margins. Memory producers are generating gross margins of roughly 80%, more than double their historical average. “Margin expansion has accounted for a large share of recent semiconductor earnings growth, but that boost should fade going forward,” Snider writes. title: Will European Gas Prices Keep Rising This Winter? - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. As the winter heating season approaches, ongoing disruptions to the flow of liquefied natural gas (LNG) from the Middle East and low storage levels in Northwest Europe are expected to keep European gas prices high, according to Goldman Sachs Research. The price of LNG in Europe has risen around 70% since July to €73 per megawatt hour (MWh) as of September 21. Prices have been volatile amid shifting news flow around the Middle East conflict, including a recent selloff of more than 10%. Our commodities analysts expect prices to average €70/MWh in the fourth quarter of 2026—well above the range of around €30–€60/MWh from before this summer. Exports of LNG from the Persian Gulf are still only at an estimated 15%–25% of their levels from before the outbreak of war between Iran and the US and Israel in February 2026. In the absence of an improvement in exports through the Strait of Hormuz, European gas prices need to increase in order to outcompete importers of LNG elsewhere in the world, says Samantha Dart, co-head of Global Commodities Research. “If others stop buying, there is more left to come to Europe,” Dart explains. The steep increase in European gas prices this summer has already started to reduce demand for gas elsewhere in the world, Dart says: Purchases of LNG declined in August in Asia and even in South America. “The process is working, but it does make natural gas very expensive,” Dart says. We spoke with Dart about her forecast for European gas prices this winter, how clients are responding to increased volatility, and the longer-term outlook for LNG. Have European gas prices risen high enough that the market is in balance now, or do you expect more increases ahead? To answer that question, we need to make an assumption on what happens with Middle East volumes. If Persian Gulf LNG exports can gradually improve over the course of the winter and normalize by early next year, then yes—the rally we have seen is enough if it’s sustained through the end of the year. That's why we raised our forecast for European LNG prices in Q4 to €70/MWh instead of the previous forecast of €53/MWh—because the demand destruction created by the recent rally needs to continue for the next few months. However, if we end up with very low winter exports out of the Persian Gulf, then this rally is not enough, and we estimate that prices would need to go above €100 a megawatt hour in peak winter to destroy even more demand outside of Europe. If a new deal between the US and Iran resulted in higher flows through the Strait, we think that prices could come back down fairly quickly. Peak winter prices could be about €50/MWh—so significantly lower than where we are today—and could move even lower in early 2027. The downside is significant and could happen fast. Heating season in Europe begins in November. How do you expect that to play out in gas prices? The main use of natural gas in the winter is for heating purposes, so the temperature can swing demand for natural gas in the winter to the tune of about 12% of storage capacity. The impact that can have on your inventories is quite meaningful. Gas storage in Northwest Europe has been filling up more slowly than expected ahead of the winter, and we expect inventories to be 19% full by the end of March 2027 assuming ten-year average winter temperatures. The risk to prices can go both ways. We estimate that weather can be powerful enough to raise our average winter price forecast about 75% if we end up with a winter that is one standard deviation colder than average. And in turn, if we end up with a winter that is one standard deviation warmer than average, our winter price assumption could drop about 30%. Why do oil exports from the Persian Gulf seem to be returning to their pre-war levels faster than gas exports? We have seen a faster normalization of flows in crude oil than in LNG. A lot of tankers are shuttling oil back and forth across the Strait—some of them with their signals off. When they reach the other side, they do a ship-to-ship transfer, and the other ship carries the oil away. This adaptation has been enough to take Persian Gulf exports of oil to about two-thirds of pre-war levels. But the same is not the case for LNG. One possible explanation is that LNG burns at higher temperatures than oil, making it more dangerous for the crew in case of an attack. Also, ship-to-ship transfers are technically more complicated for LNG, because you have to keep the LNG under very cold temperatures—around -160° celsius—so that it stays liquid. You need calm waters and a very precisely measured process for ship-to-ship transfers, so it's not as easy. And because LNG tankers are so specialized, your fleet usually does not have spare capacity. You can't afford to have LNG tankers damaged and hit by attacks. I think all of these things together end up creating a more cautious and a much slower adaptation process for LNG than for crude oil. That doesn't mean that volumes can't increase. In fact, we saw a pretty big increase in the flow of LNG out of the Strait in a matter of just four weeks after the June memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran, from around 10% of normal to 39% of normal. Are clients hedging for higher European gas prices this winter? I've been talking to European industrial clients and investors throughout this conflict. If you're an industrial user of natural gas, prices were more moderate at the beginning of the conflict, which made hedging easier. The problem is that now, when they look at how high winter prices already are, those prices are not an attractive hedge: No board is excited to approve a hedging operation at these levels. I would say hedging has somewhat paused. And from an investor point of view, you've had a somewhat similar shift. Even though they agree that the risk is skewed to the upside for European natural gas, they don't necessarily want to add long positions, because they’re worried that a headline could turn things around. Until recently, there wasn’t a lot of appetite, and the funds that did want to enter positions did so using options to reduce their risk: Call spreads are a common instrument for getting exposure. What is your longer-term outlook for natural gas prices? The current crisis aside, longer-term global LNG balances are looking increasingly oversupplied. A lot of new LNG supply is currently being built in the US and in Qatar. That means prices in the back end of the curve can move a lot lower, in our view: We forecast the price of European natural gas to decline to €19/MWh on average in 2030–2035. But we need the Strait to be open for that view to play out. So investors seeking exposure to this bearish longer-term view are using options such as puts to express the bearish view while protecting against the near-term risk of price increases. title: 2027 BMW R 12 G/S First Look: Heritage With a Heartbeat - Top Speed
content: With a Master's degree in English Literature and six years of writing experience, Aayush has been contributing to TopSpeed for over two years. Since 95% of his personality is motorcycles, he goes beyond the spec sheet to explore the culture and spirit of motorcycling. Subscribe to the TopSpeed newsletter to never miss an update Earlier this year, BMW added a new member to its R 12 lineup: the 2027 BMW R 12 G/S, a retro lite-ADV built for “purist enduro fun.” Inspired by the original BMW R 80 G/S, the new G/S combines old-school dual-sport design with an air/oil-cooled boxer engine, modern features, and an MSRP of $17,095. Inspired by the iconic 1980 R 80 G/S, often considered the world’s first adventure bike, the BMW R 12 G/S is a modern reinterpretation of the original BMW GS. The G/S name stands for Gelände / Straße, German for off-road / street, hinting at the bike’s all-round qualities. The old-school boxer engine is said to deliver a torque-rich power band. The design and engine are where this Beemer’s likeness to the first BMW GS ends, as everything else is modern, including the fully adjustable suspension, tubeless cross-spoke wheels, cornering-enabled rider aids, and available equipment such as cruise control, bidirectional quickshifter, adaptive headlights, and more. Here’s what the BMW R 12 G/S has in stock for retro ADV and BMW G/S enthusiasts. The modern G/S is built around an old-school air/oil 1,170cc boxer engine that traces its roots back to the 2008 BMW HP2 Sport. The engine features dual overhead cams, which allow it to rev higher, and a central counterbalancer shaft that dampens the flat-twin’s vibrations. It delivers 109 hp at 7,000 rpm and 85 lb-ft of torque at 6,500 rpm, with a top speed of 130 mph. The 6-speed transmission uses a hydraulically operated single-disc dry clutch and an available bidirectional quickshifter, sending power to the rear wheel via a Cardan shaft final drive. The left-hand exhaust system with a high-mount silencer is said to deliver a unique sound signature and a classic enduro look. The engine sits in a one-piece steel trellis frame with a bolt-on rear steel trellis subframe. BMW says the steering head is slightly higher and further forward on the new R 12 G/S, though it doesn’t specify the reference model. Presumably, that's the standard BMW R 12. The update lengthens the wheelbase, offering high-speed stability. This retro BMW ADV tips the scales at 504 pounds, road-ready and fully fuelled. The retro G/S also features long-travel Enduro suspension as standard. Up front is a fully adjustable 45mm upside-down fork with 8.2 inches of travel, complemented by a fully adjustable Paralever swingarm and angled monoshock with 7.8 inches of travel. With 9.4 inches of ground clearance, the manufacturer claims the suspension delivers precise, direct ride quality typical of BMW driving dynamics. Staying true to its off-road heritage, the bike features tubeless aluminum cross-spoke wheels. The 21-inch front wheel is well-suited to rough terrain, while the 17-inch rear wheel can be upgraded to an 18-inch with the Enduro Package Pro for better off-road capability. Braking duties are handled by dual 310mm discs up front and a 265mm disc at the back, all gripped by 2-piston Brembo floating calipers. The BMW R 12 G/S features a flat solo seat 33.85 inches off the ground with the standard 17-inch rear wheel. BMW says the seat’s design allows freedom of movement, making it suited to off-road riding. BMW also offers an optional Pillion Package for two-up riding that keeps the rider's seat height at 33.85 inches and a Rallye Seat that raises the seat height by 0.78 inches with a straight contour for more off-road comfort and control. As standard, the G/S’ footpegs are designed for on-road use, but their serrated profile is said to make them suitable for off-road riding as well. The butted aluminum handlebars are adjustable for improved ergonomic comfort. The rear frame also features two steel eyelets that serve as lashing points for securing light luggage. The BMW ADV's retro cockpit features a classically designed round instrument cluster and a 12V socket on the right-hand side. ConnectedRide Control is optional and adds a smartphone holder and a USB-C port to the cockpit. The bike also features a full LED lighting setup, including a 5.75-inch-diameter headlight with a signature X-shaped DRL and an available adaptive headlight. The R 12 G/S features 3 riding modes: Rain, Road, and Enduro. There’s also lean-sensitive traction control, which can be completely switched off, while ABS can be disabled only at the rear. The engine drag torque control prevents the rear wheel from losing traction during abrupt deceleration or rapid downshifting. BMW also offers the Enduro Package Pro, which adds off-road-ready accessories, including Enduro footpegs with an enlarged contact area and 3 rows of spikes for better off-road grip, as well as a 20mm handlebar riser. Other add-ons include off-road tires, a larger 18-inch rear wheel, a large engine guard, hand protection, and a longer side stand. The available Comfort package adds a bidirectional quickshifter, cruise control, hill start control, and heated grips. The R 12 G/S can also be optioned with the following: The BMW R 12 G/S sits between neo-retro scramblers and Dakar-inspired adventure bikes, but it lacks a real competitor except for the Triumph Scrambler 1200 XE, at least for off-road capability and sticker price. With an MSRP of $16,595, the Brit scrambler features an 89-horsepower parallel-twin, almost 10 inches of fully adjustable suspension travel, higher-spec Brembo brakes, and a 21/17-inch wheel setup. However, its 34.24-inch seat height is higher, making it less accessible to shorter motorcyclists, especially while off-roading. Compared to the Scrambler, the R 12 G/S offers a unique low-slung boxer engine that lowers its center of gravity and a more compact overall package. It also delivers more power while having a lower seat height. However, as with any BMW, expect the price to quickly jump from around $17,095 to over $20,000 as you tick the options boxes. title: Fire 90-82 Valkyries (Sep 22, 2026) Game Recap - ESPN
content: PORTLAND, Ore. -- — Carla Leite made the tiebreaking basket with 1:57 left in overtime and then converted a three-point play with 26.5 seconds to play as the Portland Fire ended the season with a 90-82 victory over the Golden State Valkyries on Tuesday night. Leite finished with 18 points for the Fire (17-27), who snapped a four-game losing streak. Bridget Carleton led the Fire with 26 points, including five 3-pointers. Gabby Williams had 17 points for Golden State (31-12), which led 17-0 but had its six-game winning streak snapped. The loss clinched the No. 1 seed in the playoffs for the Minnesota Lynx. The teams traded free throws and 3-pointers to open overtime before Leite's layup gave the Fire an 84-82 lead. Kaila Charles missed a 3-point attempt for the Valkyries before Leite's step-back 20-foot jumper and free throw put Portland up 87-82. The Fire made free throws the rest of the way for the final margin. Tiffany Hayes' 3-pointer gave Golden State a 75-68 with 2:13 left in regulation. Portland closed the gap on a pair of layups from Carleton and Megan DiLeo, and Leite's driving layup and free throw pulled Portland ahead 77-75. Williams' layup tied it at 77 but she missed an off-balance jumper to send the game to overtime. Carleton hit a 3-pointer with 3:20 left in the first quarter to stop the Valkyries' game-opening run. Golden State led 24-10 at the end of the first quarter. Portland clawed back into the game, closing the margin to 29-26 after DiLeo's layup and free throw. DiLeo added another layup and free throw to tie the game at 35 with 33 seconds left in the first half. The Valkyries closed out the half with a 40-37 lead. The teams wrestled for the lead in the third quarter but Golden State held a 61-58 advantage going into the fourth. Valkyries: Visit Los Angeles on Thursday, the final day of the regular season.

title: IMPC: Samantha Tan recovers through the field before setback ends Indianapolis charge - racers-behindthehelmet.com
content: Samantha Tan endured a mixed IMSA Pilot Challenge outing at Indianapolis, with the Canadian climbing from 24th to 15th in the opening stint before a setback brought her progress to an end and ultimately left the #38 ST Racing by Random Vandals BMW M4 GT4 27th in GS. Samantha Tan endured a mixed IMSA Pilot Challenge outing at Indianapolis, with the Canadian climbing from 24th to 15th in the opening stint before an off-track incident brought her progress to an end and ultimately left the #38 ST Racing by Random Vandals BMW M4 GT4 27th in GS. Tan's first stint had been one of the strongest drives for the #38 BMW, as she made steady progress through the field amid a series of early cautions and was running as high as 15th before the incident forced the car into the pits and left it two laps behind. Bill Auberlen subsequently recovered a handful of positions in the closing stages, but the result could not reflect the pace shown by Tan before the setback. Indianapolis came at the end of a particularly busy period for Tan, who had returned to Europe just one week earlier to compete in the Supercar Challenge at Hockenheim, Germany, making her return to GT3 machinery before heading back to the United States for her primary 2026 campaign in the IMSA Michelin Pilot Challenge GS class. The Canadian stepped up to GS this season, joining Auberlen at ST Racing by Random Vandals in the #38 BMW M4 GT4. Tan had already demonstrated that she could compete with the highly competitive GS field, securing back-to-back top-ten finishes at Laguna Seca and Mid-Ohio, while subsequent outings at Watkins Glen, Canadian Tire Motorsport Park, Road America and Virginia International Raceway had continued to show potential despite mechanical problems and misfortunes preventing the pairing from consistently converting their pace into the results they were targeting. On Saturday Tan took responsibility for qualifying the #38 BMW. She set a 1:31.257 to place 26th in the GS class, leaving the ST Racing by Random Vandals entry to start the two-hour race from 24th in class. Tan made a cautious but clean opening lap, finding herself boxed in through Turn 1 but avoiding the trouble around her. She moved up to 23rd shortly afterwards and became involved in a battle with the #64 CSM Porsche of Houk for position, before fighting her way past Hampton to reclaim 23rd. The first caution arrived after ten minutes when Chaves spun the Toyota Supra into the barriers at Turn 7, triggering a full-course yellow. Tan took advantage of the restart to move into 21st, continuing to make steady progress as the race settled. The green-flag running was again short-lived, however, as the leading TCR entry, the #77 Stallion Motorsports Cupra, suffered a front-suspension failure at Turn 1, immediately bringing out another caution. Racing resumed on lap 13, with Tan continuing her forward progress. A Toyota was tagged into a spin in the middle of the pack shortly afterwards but was able to rejoin without another interruption, while Ward was forced to pit with damage. Tan climbed to 19th as she continued to move forward wth determination. Another major incident involving the #66 Aston Martin and several other cars, including the #46 Team TGM Mustang, brought out a further full-course yellow. Some drivers were forced to take evasive action, once again compressing the field and creating another opportunity for Tan to gain ground. The third restart produced another strong run from the Canadian, who climbed to 17th and continued improving her lap times as the field settled. Tan was soon circulating in the 1:32.5 range and continued to move forward, eventually reaching 15th position. At the 40-minute mark, the first scheduled pit stops were beginning to unfold and Tan initially remained on track, giving the team an opportunity to gain further track position through the strategy. The BMW was therefore in a promising position, with Tan having made significant progress from her starting place and running 15th in class. Unfortunately, the race changed dramatically moments later; the #38 BMW slid through the gravel, bringing out another full-course yellow and ending Tan's strong opening stint. The incident forced the BMW to be towed back to the pits, where Auberlen was able to take over the car, but the time lost during the recovery left the ST Racing entry effectively two laps down and 28th in GS. The race returned to green with 55 minutes remaining, leaving Auberlen with a difficult recovery task. The veteran driver settled into the 1:32s and began working his way back through the field, closing in on Kris Wilson's #64 Ford. Wilson was only around two seconds ahead and Auberlen was almost a second per lap quicker on lap 51. He rapidly closed the gap and completed the pass over the following laps, moving the #38 into 26th position. Auberlen continued to circulate strongly but the deficit left the BMW with limited opportunities to recover further positions. He made his final pit stop with 12 minutes remaining and rejoined in 28th. The race was interrupted once more with five minutes remaining when overall leader Gabby Chaves, who had not yet completed his final pit stop, slowed after running out of fuel and stopped on track, triggering another full-course yellow. Rain was also beginning to appear around the circuit, adding another variable to the final stages. Auberlen was able to gain one further position during the restart, moving into 27th before the chequered flag. The result was ultimately not representative of what had been a very promising first stint for Tan. Starting 24th, she had made her way through a chaotic opening phase of the race and climbed as high as 15th before the incident. Despite the Indianapolis setback, Tan and Auberlen continue to build experience together in Tan's first GS campaign, with the #38 pairing having now collected 1,360 points after nine rounds of the 2026 IMSA Michelin Pilot Challenge season. Team Germany (Men’s) and Team Europe (Women’s) won the 10th BMW Motorrad International GS Trophy, held in Romania September 13-18. The qualifying rounds did not include the USA this year; however, two Americans qualified through the open International Qualifier, held at Enduro Park Hechlingen in Germany last year. Representing the USA on Team International were Stephanie Townsend in the Women’s division and Jordan Wiley in Men’s. This year’s edition was more technical than ever, with narrow forest trails, washed-out mountain paths, riverbeds and high-altitude routes. After six days and approximately 930 miles, Team Germany (Fabi Fenner, Norman Pleissner, Flo Thomann) won the Men’s competition with 203 points, while Team Europe (Chrissie Harcourt and Anja Filak) won the Women’s competition with 200 points. The Women’s competition was decided only in the final challenge, with Colorado’s Townsend and teammate Eduarda “Duda” Mikulski from Brazil on Team International entering the final day ahead of Team Europe by just two points. “We were certainly the smallest team in the competition,” Anja Filak, Team Europe, said. “But we rode like one body, as one unit. Chrissie is amazing. She gave me a lot of advice, and I was able to follow her and make it through. I gained more confidence because I knew I could follow her and stay focused. I took everything she told me over these days very much to heart and tried to put every piece of advice into practice – and it worked!” “I can hardly describe this feeling,” Chrissie Harcourt, Team Europe, said. “My head is a little all over the place; everything feels a bit shaky. It will take a while for it to truly sink in. Speaking at the Barclays 24th Annual Global Financial Services Conference, chairman and CEO David Solomon highlighted that the company expects its revenue base to reach roughly $70 billion this year, up from the mid-$30 billion range when its strategic plan began in 2018–19. The expansion reflects growth across core businesses, a more diversified revenue mix and improving operating leverage. A key pillar of GS’s strategy has been reducing the dependence on more cyclical revenue streams and building a broader and more durable earnings base. The company now centers its growth strategy around two major franchises — Global Banking & Markets (“GBM”) and Asset & Wealth Management (“AWM”). In GBM, Goldman continues to capitalize on its strong positions in investment banking, equities and FICC, while expanding financing activities. In the first half of 2026, Global Banking & Markets revenues climbed 35% to $28.26 billion, led by robust investment banking and Equities activity. AWM is also becoming an increasingly important source of recurring revenues. The business is growing faster than its targeted high-single-digit pace, with roughly $4 trillion in assets under supervision. Goldman is expanding wealth management, alternatives and private credit, while targeting a 30% margin and high-teen returns. Alternatives fundraising is expected to exceed $125 billion in 2026. The company is also benefiting from stronger operating leverage. Management expects roughly 6% revenue growth to translate into a more than 10% earnings increase, supported by scale, automation and productivity initiatives. Continued investments in technology and process redesign could provide further scope for margin expansion. Financial trends underscore this progress. Since Goldman’s first Investor Day in 2020, firmwide net revenues have increased roughly 60%, while more durable revenues have doubled. Momentum strengthened further in the first half of 2026, with firmwide net revenues rising 27% year over year. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for 2026 revenues is pegged at $71.6 billion, indicating year-over-year growth of 22.9% and broadly aligning with management’s expectations for a revenue base of nearly $70-billion range. GS’s push toward a roughly $70-billion revenue base underscores the progress of its multi-year transformation. Growth in Asset & Wealth Management, financing, and other durable revenue streams, combined with ongoing efficiency initiatives, should support stronger earnings growth and improved margins over time. title: BMW R1300 GS Adventure gets colourful Oktoberfest makeover - Visordown
content: BMW Motorrad has given an R 1300 GS Adventure a colourful Oktoberfest makeover, creating a one-off Wiesn-GS for Munich’s 2026 celebrations. There are few things more German than a GS Adventure, but BMW Motorrad has managed to make its big adventure bike even more Bavarian, thanks to a colourful Oktoberfest makeover. Meet the BMW R1300 GS Adventure x Oktoberfest München 2026, a one-off version of the big GS created specifically for this year’s beer-fuelled celebrations in Munich. Rather than launching another special edition with a few extra accessories and a new badge, BMW has taken an R1300 GS Adventure Triple Black and given it a rather more obvious makeover. The work was carried out with German customisation company ARider, which has covered the bike in a wrap inspired by the official Oktoberfest 2026 poster. The design uses the colours, shapes and graphics from the poster across the GS Adventure’s bodywork, giving it a look that is considerably more colourful than the usually stealthy Triple Black. BMW describes the finished bike as an ‘Unikat’, which is German for one-off. That means this sadly isn't a GS you’ll be able to order from your local BMW dealer. Underneath the Oktoberfest graphics, it remains a standard R1300 GS Adventure. That means BMW’s 1,300cc boxer engine producing 145bhp at 7,750rpm and 149Nm of torque at 6,500rpm, along with the big 30-litre fuel tank that makes the Adventure considerably more touring-friendly than the standard GS. The Triple Black model also brings a substantial equipment list, although BMW’s Oktoberfest project is really about the appearance rather than mechanical changes. There’s no extra power, suspension trickery or performance upgrade hiding underneath the colourful wrap. The project even has its own suitably Bavarian name, with BMW referring to the bike as the ‘Wiesn-GS’. The German manufacturer has also used the phrase ‘Auf’klebt is’’, a play on the Bavarian dialect that refers to the graphics being stuck onto the bike. There’s a competition running alongside the project, too, with BMW Motorrad Germany offering the chance to win a BMW motorcycle for a weekend between 9 and 12 October 2026. title: Robot dances, volleyball autographs and ramyun: inside GS Group's fifth hackathon - 헤럴드경제
content: Employees pitch AI solutions to real workplace problems Photo booths, K-pop robot and signing session add festival feel Record 923 participants; 2,732 have taken part over five years About 30 hackathon ideas already in use at worksites Seven fully deployed, including AI safety platform AIR 'Goal is to redesign inefficient offline work through AI' Some 468 GS Group employees dressed in baseball-style uniforms gathered Monday at the Westin Seoul Parnas in Gangnam-gu for the fifth GS Group Hackathon, spending the day deep in AI solution development. The event looked nothing like a typical stiff corporate AI competition. A photo-booth machine drew a steady stream of participants, while a robot performed K-pop idol dance routines nearby. GS Caltex's KIXX women's volleyball team held an autograph session that had employees lining up to meet the players. Those who needed a break from coding stepped outside to camping chairs, where they ate ramyun by the Han River. The setup was designed to let staff focus on AI development without feeling pressured. GS Group Chairman Heo Tae-soo and GS Caltex Vice Chairman Heo Se-hong attended the event, encouraging employees and asking questions such as how they planned to apply their coding skills. They also visited booths run by participating companies — Amazon Web Services, OpenAI and Hwain Robotics — to ask about the latest technology trends. The hackathon is an annual event where GS Group employees pitch AI-powered ideas to solve real problems inside the company. The two-day event, which runs through Tuesday, is expected to draw a total of 923 participants — 797 from GS affiliates and 126 from outside the group — the largest turnout in the event's history. Cumulative participation over the past five years stands at 2,732. Kim Jin-a, the GS senior managing director who organized the event, said the company pays close attention not just to the ideas employees propose but to the problems they identify. "The agenda that comes up most often at the hackathon is safety," she said, adding that safety workers were spending so much time on paperwork that they had little time to visit actual worksites. Executives are now discussing how to address that problem, she said. This year's theme is "Play with GenAI Season 3: Build & Act" — a signal that the hackathon aims to go beyond idea generation. "Build" means producing AI tools that actually work; "Act" means connecting those tools to real operations and business sites. To help participants, GS provided AI-ready data that AI systems could use on the spot. Kim said there is broad internal consensus that hackathon experiments play an important role in driving change on the ground. "We felt the pace of moving from experiment to real-world application needed to pick up, which is why we chose 'Build & Act' as the theme," she said. About 30 ideas generated through GS hackathons are already being applied at worksites, seven of them fully deployed. The standout example is AIR (AI Risk Assessment), proposed by GS Power employees at the third hackathon. AIR takes a task name and a brief description as inputs and automatically identifies potential hazards, assigns risk ratings and suggests preventive safety measures. The platform is now in use at more than 330 worksites across GS and beyond. A real-time temperature and humidity monitoring alert system being introduced by GS Power, and an AI-based design risk inspection tool at GS Retail, also trace their origins to hackathon proposals. "As the AIR case shows, we are entering an era where employees on the ground can solve problems directly through AI," Kim said. "Starting this year, helping more programs reach actual worksites is our main goal." Underpinning employees' ability to build AI programs with relative ease is Miso, GS Group's in-house AI transformation platform. Used at the hackathon itself, Miso is designed to help staff create AI-related tools without specialized expertise. Kim said employees have used the platform to attempt development of more than 20,000 AI programs. "GS aims to redesign offline work processes through AI," she said. "Certain tasks may be delegated to AI, but that does not mean employees are being replaced." She added that because frontline workers carry heavy workloads, AI handles inefficient tasks on their behalf.

title: GS Group chairman calls for continued workplace innovation through AI tools - 헤럴드경제
content: Chairman Heo Tae-soo attends for second consecutive year 'Not many companies solve field problems through coding,' he says GS Caltex Vice Chairman Heo Se-hong also takes part GS Group Chairman Heo Tae-soo said it represents "significant progress" when frontline employees identify and solve problems on their own using AI — something he said sets GS apart from most companies. Heo made the remarks Monday at the 5th GS Group Hackathon, held at the Westin Seoul Parnas in Gangnam-gu. "Not many companies around the world directly solve field problems through coding and similar tools," he said. The hackathon is an event where GS employees pitch ideas for boosting workplace productivity and driving other innovations using AI. A total of 923 people are expected to participate through Tuesday, including 797 employees from GS affiliates and 126 outside participants — the largest turnout in the event's history. Cumulative attendance over the past five years has reached 2,732. Heo, who also attended last year's event, has shown a particular affinity for the hackathon. "It is meaningful to see the hackathon grow," Heo said, adding that President Lee Jae Myung praised GS when the two met at Cheong Wa Dae earlier this year. "President Lee already knew about GS's AIR — AI Risk Assessment — and gave us a lot of credit for it," he said. AIR is a safety-management AI agent that originated as an idea at the 3rd GS Group Hackathon in 2024. When a user enters a task name and brief description, the AI automatically identifies potential hazards, assigns risk ratings and suggests preventive safety measures. GS has distributed AIR free of charge to more than 330 worksites, including small and midsize businesses. President Lee praised GS for its contribution to resolving safety issues at smaller companies. Heo said that in the past, employees who needed a digital tool had to submit a request to the IT department and wait for developers to deliver results. "Now, the people who know the field best can build anything they need through AI," he said. He added that ideas generate even greater value when applied and spread across the workplace, and expressed hope that employees would use AI as a basic tool to drive innovation in their work. GS Caltex Vice Chairman Heo Se-hong, who also attended the event, said in his opening remarks that GS must become the company best at solving real-world problems customers face using new technology. "This does not start with sweeping change," he said. "It begins with small attempts — members questioning existing ways of doing things and putting new ideas into action." Heo went on to reference Carrier Pigeon, a slow-messaging app gaining popularity in the United States. The app delays message delivery in proportion to the physical distance between users — if the recipient is on the other side of the world, a message can take days to arrive. "This app offers people worn out by constant notifications and instant communication the pleasure of waiting," Heo said. "In the AI era, what ultimately matters is being clear about whose problems you are solving and what those problems are." He added that AI will advance far more rapidly going forward, and that technologies that seem novel today will soon become ordinary tools anyone can use. "Ultimately, competitiveness comes from internalizing the process of identifying problems and solving them with new technology," he said.

title: GS Engineering & Construction builds pre-verification center for construction robots - 헤럴드경제
content: Workers, materials and sequential processes all factored in Construction sites push ahead with physical AI adoption GS Engineering & Construction announced Tuesday that it has established a proof-of-concept center to comprehensively verify the performance and operational viability of new technologies and construction robots before deploying them at actual job sites. The center was created by remodeling part of the company's technology research institute in Yongin, Gyeonggi Province. It goes beyond one-off performance tests of individual robots, providing a dedicated space to identify and address the wide range of variables that can arise when applying technology to the unpredictable conditions of a construction site. Through the proof-of-concept process, the center rigorously examines how workers and robots divide responsibilities, as well as work sequences, movement routes and operating conditions, and puts in place the integrated processes required for real-world deployment. The center is currently running active tests on a range of construction robots, including a concrete leveling robot. The company independently verifies each robot's work accuracy, productivity and site-readiness, focusing on processes that demand both quality and efficiency simultaneously — such as achieving floor flatness after concrete is poured. GS Engineering & Construction plans to evaluate the center's results and utilization before pursuing the opening of additional centers with enhanced capabilities and expanded scale. Unlike a manufacturing factory, where work takes place on a standardized production line, a construction site is a quintessentially unstructured environment in which workspaces, movement routes, personnel and materials shift continuously as each phase of work progresses. For this reason, even the most capable robot will struggle to deliver real productivity gains on site unless it accounts for workers' existing tasks, material delivery and movement paths, and potential interference with preceding and subsequent work phases. That is why GS Engineering & Construction focuses not simply on introducing robots and AI, but on how to integrate those technologies seamlessly into existing construction processes. The company plans to build a virtuous cycle in which technologies are thoroughly reviewed at the pre-verification stage — covering worker fatigue reduction from repetitive-task elimination, quality consistency, safety risk reduction, the feasibility of nighttime and unmanned operations, and linkage with follow-on processes — before being deployed on live sites, with proven technologies then rolled out across other projects. To support this effort, the company also operates an in-house innovation body called the ICC (Innovation Connect Council), which systematically identifies physical AI technologies. Through the ICC, the company pinpoints productivity bottlenecks and technology needs on site, then scouts domestic and international startups and AI and robotics technologies to address them. Where necessary, it pursues joint technology development or investment alongside the proof-of-concept process before applying solutions in the field. In addition, GS Engineering & Construction maintains ongoing exchanges with construction companies, robotics firms and research institutions at home and abroad, sharing practical case studies and know-how on technology application at job sites, while expanding collaboration with overseas companies on technology exchange, promising-technology identification and investment linkages. "The key is not simply bringing robots to a site, but identifying technologies that match the site's actual needs and naturally embedding them into existing construction processes through thorough pre-verification," a company official said. "The ultimate goal is to simultaneously raise productivity, safety and cost competitiveness." Meanwhile, GS Engineering & Construction posted an operating profit of 232.4 billion won ($168 million) in the first half of this year, up 41.8 percent from 164.2 billion won in the same period last year.

Tucker York: I think I've got a couple of pages of introduction of you, Ryan, but we've decided that people here kind of know who you are, Ryan Serhant. Welcome to Goldman Sachs. Ryan Serhant: Thanks so much. Thanks for having me. Let's do this. Tucker York: Okay. A lot of people know who you are. Seen the TV. Know about the business. Know about the social media, all that kind of stuff, who you are today. I'm just interested to go back to kind of like, how did you get to this place? So, grew up in the Boston area. Went to Hamilton College. What about the background informs who we have in front of us today? Ryan Serhant: I was always a storyteller. If you ask my parents what my superpower is, they'll say that Ryan could tell stories. And I don't know why, I think it's just a part of my genetics. And so, that kind of morphed into having an interest in theater. My whole family is in finance, but I was always telling stories. And so, when I moved to New York City 20 years ago this month actually in 2006, that's what I wanted to do. And I wanted to do it on stage. Really, really hard to make money. Ran out of money really, really quick. And then I got my real estate license only because I didn't have to go to one spot every day. I didn't want to wait tables or bartend. I didn't really want to go back to school. And I definitely, definitely did not want to move home with my parents. I went home for that Thanksgiving. It was Thanksgiving of 2008. And I was going through my day and some of the rental clients that I was meeting in Bronx and Harlem and everything. And I just remember looking up, and I have three sisters and two brothers, and everyone was just staring at me. I was like, what? And my little brother goes, "Dude, you've changed." I'm like, "What do you mean? I haven't changed." He's like, "You talk so fast now." Like, "I don't talk fast. You talk slow. Maybe you should move to New York. In a New York minute we got deals to do. I got money to make. Let's go." And so, I think I'm a bit of a product of my environment. You know, New York City is an incredibly intellectually curious ecosystem. And it enables you to shoot for the stars. But it will also provide you the opportunity to bury yourself in the pavement. And I think it gives you the tools to work as hard as you possibly can to build as much as you can. So, to answer your question, I don't think I thought about it that much. I knew theater is what I liked. I liked performing. I liked being in front of the camera. I liked being on stage. And I just hustled and did auditions all day long. I got into a soap opera. Then they killed me. I was a pretty famous hand model for a while. Ryan Serhant: I'm dually talented, man. I was born with two of these babies. I'm very thankful. And so, that paid the rent a little bit. And then it just got to the point where I needed to figure out what to do with my life. I wanted to be successful, and I knew what it was like to be in New York City and not have money. And I never wanted to go back there. Tucker York: When I think about where you've ultimately had huge success on the real estate side, this is a tough business that requires a huge amount of perseverance, rejection, all that. Similar to what you hear about all the acting stories. I came to New York. I didn't get the role, but I kept going, I kept going, I kept going. And it sounds the way you talk about it, it was less about, I wanted to be necessarily an actor. I wanted to have enough money to be able to do something I wanted to do. Ryan Serhant: Yeah, it was-- My dad always told me, "You can quit whenever you want at anything you do, but you're only allowed to quit on your best day." And I've never forgotten that. At the end of the day, you have to do an internal check-in where you tell yourself, was today a day a bad day, a good day, or a great day. And if you don't do that, you're going to blink, and 10 years are going to go by. Right? 15 years are going to go by. And you're going to wake up in a life that you worked really, really hard to get to, that you actually resent. And that can happen really quickly, especially in New York. And so, I made very sure that I say, ready, set, go. And at the end of every day, I know where I am. And so, yeah, you quit on your best day. Tucker York: It's a good call. I'm going to get to, like, the really, really good days that follow this. But 2008 is the time when you decide this acting thing's kind of hard. It's not really going to work. I need to make some money. Kind of like, let's sell real estate at the beginning of the global financial crisis. Ryan Serhant: Yeah. It wasn't really-- I mean, yes. Looking back on it, absolute worst time possible to get into the real estate business. For me, like, I had no money. So, it was summer of 2008. I didn't know what else to do. And so, a friend said, "Get your real estate license. Meet people on Craigslist. And then you'll figure it out." All I had to do was make $2,000 a month, and I didn't have to move home. The day I got my license and started, it just so happened to be the day Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy. And to me, you know, I just thought everyone just loses their job all the time. Like, man, every client I would get. Then they would get fired a month later. And then they couldn't close, and you couldn't get a mortgage. But in retrospect, what ended up happening, because so many people got out of the business, and because I was so ignorant, and ignorance in motion wins all the time over intelligence at rest, I just moved as fast as I could. 82% of all newly licensed agents in the United States quit in the first two years. They try it and they bail because it's too hard. There's no salary. There are no benefits. You eat what you kill. Buyers are liars. And sellers will also lie to you, right? Tucker York: Again, these are the four years before you're on TV. And the reality is, you're, like, incredible. Incredibly focused, all in, cold calling. Doing all that kind of stuff all the time. Is that what made you successful? Ryan Serhant: Not at the beginning. The acting business teaches you the art of rejection. And you have to be able to take 52 punches right in the nose and say, "Thank you, sir, may I have another?" Otherwise, you can't do the bit. You have to move home. But you learn that even though people say, "I don't like you because of your face," you have to keep moving. And for me, the rejection on an apartment was never because of my hair. In fact, my hair was super helpful. Because I have an old man set of hair, but a young boy face, and especially at that time, I would meet clients, and they would look at me, and then they would look up, and they'd say, "How long have you been in this business?" Instead of saying how old are you. And I would just say, "A while." And "a while" is great marketing. So, I did a couple things. One was Craigslist ads. And I would just meet people cold. And I would post ads for apartments and have keys in my pocket and run around. Two was I would just go on the street. The best part about New York was that every single person outside was a potential client. And so, I would stand outside Saks Fifth Avenue because our office was at 20 East 49th. If you had more than two shopping bags, you could probably afford a new apartment. I had business cards back then, old school business cards, and I would say, you know, "My name is Ryan Serhant. If you're looking to buy or sell or rent in New York City, please reach out to me." Some of those people and their families are still clients to this day. Tucker York: You do the hard work during this period of time. And then you catch this gig on TV. Ryan Serhant: Luck is what happens when opportunity meets hard work. And hard work trumps luck when luck doesn't work hard. And so, I'd spent my entire life thinking I was going to do X. And it didn't work out for me. And instead of treating it like a brick wall, which a lot of people do, I treat every obstacle like a speed bump. In the grand scheme of life, it's just a speed bump. Just keep driving. That's what I did when theater didn't work out and got into real estate. I put theater to the side. I put acting to the side. And then there was an open casting call in Times Square for Million Dollar Listing in New York in March of 2010. And I went just because why not? Why would I not go? And I'd done stuff, you know, on camera before. And 3,000 real estate agents showed up. And then they whittled us down over the course of nine months to four of us. They shot the first season of that show with all four of us. And they told us, at the beginning, "Only three of you will make the final cut. So, be good." And so, I just did what I've always done. I just buckled down, and I just grinded, and I knew the one thing that I had was a relentless sense of optimism. Even in our company today, optimism is not a personality trait. It is an operational discipline. Everything can be bad for everybody all the time. There are always ups. There are always downs. But you've got to make a choice every day, today is going to be great, and here's why. And then the show happened, and, you know, ran for 10 years. Tucker York: So, by the way, the optimism thing, too, it's infectious. Ryan Serhant: Selling is a transfer of enthusiasm in whatever it is you're selling. Tucker York: So, you're on TV. The TV helps the real estate, helps the TV, right? Tucker York: Things are going legitimately great for you until we get to the next global crisis, COVID, and you decide, hey, let's end this and start a company. What's the motivation? Is it greed? Is it fear? Ryan Serhant: By 2018, I had the number one residential selling real estate team in New York City history. I had four television shows. I was writing my first book. I had all this stuff that I was doing, and I didn't know what was next. Am I just going to sell real estate? And also, I saw that the world was starting to change. I saw that real estate was moving from being something that was searchable to something that was discoverable. I have never used my company for distribution ever, because in Instagram and in YouTube, where we started doing property tours and promoting real estate at a social level in 2013 and 2014, I could generate more qualified eyeballs for a singular property in ten minutes than any other firm could ever pay for combined. And most people start businesses, I think, completely backwards. They say, "I want to make a profit. How do I make profit? I'm going to create a product. Great. How do I do that? I need people. Okay, why are people going to work for me?" And for me, I did it literally the exact opposite. I have a clear purpose. I'm going to align that with the right people. If you believe in what I'm doing, great. If you don't, you don't have to work for me. We can then sell any product to make all the profit. Tucker York: So, but tell us. Describe SERHANT beyond, if you will. Just the real estate brokerage that it is, but it's other things. Ryan Serhant: Yeah, we have four key businesses. One is the brokerage, which predominantly operates in the cloud. We operate in 17 states. We'll operate in about 25 states by the end of the year. You know, we do about right now just over a billion dollars a month in transactions. We then have Sellit.com, which is our education business. We have Studios, which is our in-house production studio, which is our top of funnel lead generator. So, we create more content for real estate than any other firm on earth combined per month, and we use that to generate organic lead flow. So, our customer acquisition cost is zero. Tucker York: Just because we talked about this before, compare that to other people's customer acquisition cost. Ryan Serhant: You buy them. I mean, you have to buy revenue. Tucker York: The model is to spend millions of dollars advertising stuff, right? Ryan Serhant: Yeah. You advertise to buy customers. And for real estate agents, right, you have to buy them as well. You have to incentivize them to come to you. We buy zero people. We've never bought a single real estate agent ever. People leave tons and tons of money on the table at other firms, and they come to us, and they win with us. I think that's why our agents are the best of the best in the markets that we're in. One of the reasons I also was excited to be asked to be here today, too, is I use the Goldman analogy a lot, right? My interest is not in being the biggest. It is just in being the best. And if I can provide the absolute best service with the best people to the best clients, you can create a pretty great and differentiated company that way. And then they're S.MPLE. S.MPLE is, think of it as, you know, Uber for the home transaction. So, we have technology that empowers the driver who are agents. My goal is to build a transaction platform that is consumer-facing that grabs that $400 trillion total addressable market, right? In the only AI vertical way that you've ever been able to create. I mean, the technology that we have today will solve the greatest problem I've ever had as a real estate agent, which is, how do I take 129 steps and put it in one thing to get a home sold? And you just could never do it until, like, nine months ago. Tucker York: People-intensive business, relationships will still matter, I assume. Ryan Serhant: Yes. Yeah, it doesn't replace trust. I sold a house, a series of houses, last year for $308 million. The most expensive residential transaction in all of 2025 in the United States to somebody very much in the AI space. And he was very, very interested in sales as a skill set that is irreplaceably human. Tucker York: He was studying your Jedi mind tricks. Ryan Serhant: Yeah, my goal with AI, and I think everyone's goal, is how do you superpower human skill so that you can do what you do best and you can actually have more time to build those relationships and build that trust with your clients. Tucker York: Comments about the real estate market today. I find that real estate people say, "Oh, this is the best time to buy and it's the best time to sell," right? Ryan Serhant: Always. Everyone's business is great until it's not. And so, when it rains, grab your buckets. And we are definitely in a bifurcated housing market. And I hardly ever actually use the phrase "housing market" because I really do think we have a housing obstacle course in this country with how difficult and kind of friction the process is. But you have people who can pay cash and you have everybody else. And it used to have parity. Because you have people who would pay cash because they could, but then it was easy and relatively inexpensive to get a mortgage. For the past four years, it has not been so. Inventory is at all-time-lows, year after year after year. But you're starting to see some of that wake up. People have life changes and they adjust to a new normal, which is happening now. Transaction volume is high. The super luxury market is incredibly high. There are massive transactions that are happening all over the country. The first-time home buyer market is incredibly well funded by their parents. So, they've been doing a great job as well. And we continue to move forward. You know, we don't have a housing crisis. We have a housing supply issue. We just have to create more supply. We have to create tax credits. We do commercial now at our company, which is really interesting. So, you're starting to see municipalities start to release kind of derelict office buildings, space they don't have, which is great for the repurpose into residential space. And so, we're doing a lot of that too, to try to do our part to solve the problem. Tucker York: So, we're a large company, we've been around for a long time. And there's a big mentorship culture here and people that have been around here for a long time. Tucker York: And the people that have been around here for a long time also knew it was like when they came in. And so, it's a pay it forward kind of thing. You didn't really have that experience. You're kind of self-taught. Who are the people that kind of help you? How do you get that input? Ryan Serhant: When I started, I had none at all. Everyone told me not to get into real estate. Everyone told me not to do Million Dollar Listing. Everyone for sure told me not to start my own company. And I went the exact opposite way. I have a lot of great clients, incredibly successful clients, that I can call at any time and ask them for advice. But also, I'm only ever going to catch myself. Like I've got to stare at myself in the mirror every day. And so, I'm the one who's going to take the risk. And if things go well, it's because of everybody else. And if things go poorly, it's 100% my fault. And that's the deal I made with myself when I came to New York City. And that's the deal I made with myself when we started the company. You know, my ambition when I first came to the city was, let me figure this out. I've got to try it. I'd rather regret the things I did than the things I never tried. Let's move. Today, I think people confuse my ambition with responsibility. Because if you knew how many other people really win when I win, you'd understand that it's not for Ryan. It's for everybody else. I surround myself with people far smarter than me every single day. I hire intrapreneurs. So, the same way if you're ever building a team or anyone here who's hiring, you want to hire people that, one, make you a little bit afraid because they're so good and they're going to take your job. Otherwise, why work with them? And two, that you're going to be able to really, really, you know, learn from. Tucker York: What's the advice? What's the kind of the learnings in the last 20 years, what you've done, everything else you would share with people, sort of more broadly as they think about career? Ryan Serhant: My go-to is always to take care of the work. And if you take care of the work, the work will take care of you. I meet a lot of people who are very, very outcome focused, which I think is okay. It's good. But really just focusing on, like, well, I've got to get to here and here and here and here, you lose sight of why you're doing the work in the first place. And I think just doing really, really great work day in and day out, if you do that, you will be as successful as you want to be. As long as you move quickly. Speed to lead is a real thing, especially today. As well as taking calculated risks with yourself, with your career. Like, what's the worst that can happen is something that I'll always try to ask myself too. I don't know if that's great advice. But life finds a way. Tucker York: That's your point. Is if you keep working, the odds of that happening are greatly reduced, right? Ryan Serhant: I remember when I first got into real estate and I was running around, I had holes in my shoes, I was exhausted, I was sweaty all the time. And I remember my parents came and visited me in my apartment. And I was complaining about how early I have to wake up, and I'm tired, and this, that, the other. And I remember my dad saying to me, "Do you think that I wanted to go to work every day?" And that sentence, like, blew my mind, you know? Because I grew up with him at State Street in 1993. Like, of course he wanted to go to work. Like, that's what he does. He was Mr. Finance, you know? And so, I knew in that moment, like, okay, I will not complain ever again, and I will just take care of the work, and I will just continue to move forward. Tucker York: Thank you very much for coming to Goldman Sachs and, frankly, sharing a story that I know we all find pretty inspirational and pretty cool. Tucker York: Very successful. Thank you everybody. title: Unveiling Microbial Communities And Biogeochemical Cycles In Antarctic Colored Snow - Astrobiology Web
content:
[BMC Microbiology].   Snow cover, the extensive terrestrial habitat in Antarctica, sometimes exhibits vivid coloration, yet the structure and function of its microbial communities remain poorly characterized. Using metagenomic sequencing of red snow (RS) and green snow (GS) from the Fildes Peninsula, we found that bacterial, eukaryotic, and archaeal relative abundances were 85.82%, 13.52% and 0.16%, respectively. β-Diversity differed significantly between RS and GS across these three domains (P < 0.05). Dominant bacterial phyla included Bacteroidota (RS: 62.61%; GS: 38.72%) and Pseudomonadota (RS: 32.80%; GS: 54.10%). Among eukaryotes, Chlorophyta (RS: 58.10%; GS: 52.98%) and Basidiomycota (RS: 14.80%; GS: 8.08%) were prevalent. Nanobdellota dominated archaea, with lower abundance in RS than GS. In the algal community, Sanguina, Gonium and Chloromonas were significantly enriched in red snow, while Chlorella and Micractinium were enriched in green snow (P < 0.05). Marker genes associated with carbon (C), nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and sulfur (S) cycles were identified in green and red snow. Aerobic respiration and phosphate regulation were significantly enriched in red snow, while CO oxidation, fermentation, and denitrification were significantly enriched in green snow. Key microbial genera associated with these functional pathways also varied. In the denitrification of red snow, Stutzerimonas was the most abundant genus, while Janthinobacterium was abundant in green snow. Nitrification-related genes were detected only in red snow based on the present metagenomic data. The network of the red snow microbial community was potentially more complex and resistant based on topology, which not only benefited its own long-term survival but might also have potentially influenced the positive feedback effect of snowmelt by maintaining a low-albedo snow surface. This provided an ecological implication under climate warming: the expansion of red snow patches showed the potential to the increase nitrate runoff export, which would affect nitrogen nutrient levels in coastal Antarctic waters. Overall, this study used metagenomics to compare the multidomain (bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes) composition and diversity between red snow and green snow, and directly linked key microbial taxa with functional genes of biogeochemical cycles. This study provided new insights into the biological characteristics and functional potential of Antarctic colored snow.
