              send an e-mail Colțești, Romania. After six days of riding, around
  1,500 kilometres and an exceptionally demanding route through the
  Romanian Carpathians, the tenth BMW Motorrad International GS Trophy
  has been decided. Team Germany (Fabi Fenner, Norman Pleissner, Flo
  Thomann) won the men’s competition with 203 points, while Team Europe
  (Chrissie Harcourt, Anja Filak) prevailed in the women’s competition
  with 200 points. The anniversary edition went farther, higher and was
  more technical than ever before – across narrow forest trails,
  washed-out mountain paths, riverbeds and historic high-altitude
  routes. At the same time, it remained true to what defines the GS
  Trophy: a shared adventure in which team spirit, precision, endurance
  and mutual support matter more than outright speed. The outcome was decided only in the final challenge. Ahead of the
  last day, just two points separated Team International and Team Europe
  in the women’s competition, while Team Germany defended an
  eleven-point lead over Team Europe in the men’s competition. Under
  maximum pressure, the eventual winners demonstrated precisely the
  qualities that defined this GS Trophy: trust, composure and consistent teamwork. In the women’s final, Chrissie Harcourt from Great Britain and
  Anja Filak from the Netherlands rode with control and close
  coordination to secure victory for Team Europe. Team Germany,
  comprising Fabian Fenner, Norman Pleissner and Florian Thomann,
  crowned a consistently strong performance throughout the week with
  overall victory in the men’s competition. BMW Motorrad International GS Trophy 2026 Romania – Final standings.

Women’s teams:
1. Europe – 200 points2. International – 1843.
  Australia – 1644. China – 1595. Germany – 146 Men’s teams:
1. Germany – 203 points2. Europe – 1473. Ukraine –
  1444. Australia – 1385. Japan – 1356. Korea –
  1317. International – 1288. China – 102 The winners of the women’s competition, Team Europe, had not known
  each other before this event: one came from Wales in the United
  Kingdom, the other from the Netherlands. Over the course of the event,
  they grew together as a team and, with mutual support, overcame every
  obstacle on their way to victory. Chrissie Harcourt, Team Europe: “I can hardly
  describe this feeling. My head is a little all over the place;
  everything feels a bit shaky. It will take a while for it to truly
  sink in. I am incredibly proud of both of us.” Anja Filak, Team Europe: “We were certainly the
  smallest team in the competition. But we rode like one body, as one
  unit. Chrissie is amazing. She gave me a lot of advice, and I was able
  to follow her and make it through. I gained more confidence because I
  knew I could follow her and stay focused. I took everything she told
  me over these days very much to heart and tried to put every piece of
  advice into practice – and it worked!” The tenth edition set new benchmarks: six days, around 1,500
  kilometres and approximately half of the route away from paved roads.
  For three consecutive days, the teams spent eleven to twelve hours on
  the move; day three featured more than 300 kilometres, including 170
  kilometres of trails. Cold temperatures, dense fog, wet camps and
  constantly changing terrain made recovery and personal organisation
  just as important as riding skill. The most formidable challenges awaited high in the Carpathians: the
  eight-kilometre Metzeler Enduro Navigation Challenge on narrow single
  trails, the uncompromising climbs to the Strategica Mountain Road and
  an exposed descent along a narrow goat track. Riverbeds, deep fine
  gravel, wet grassy slopes and washed-out forest tracks added to the
  challenge. The combination of distance, technical difficulty,
  navigation and fatigue made Romania one of the toughest and, at the
  same time, most impressive GS Trophies to date. Another defining feature was the interplay between authentic
  adventure and international community. Under the motto “Back to
  Basics”, 30 riders from 13 nations experienced Romania’s wild
  landscapes, historic high-altitude routes and warm hospitality. The
  BMW R 12 G/S proved itself as a versatile competition bike – powerful,
  precise and controllable on every type of terrain. Munich, 13 May 2026. Watch the webcast of the public session of the 106th Annual General Meeting of BMW AG.

This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy Overview: The carving ski category is shifting: rather than narrow race-inspired sticks, most 2027 standouts run wider underfoot with more rockered tips, so lesser experts can access that locked-in, arcing feel once reserved for ex-racers. SKI tested this year’s carving skis at Deer Valley, Utah, scoring each on edge hold, hard-snow feel, and control at speed. The seven skis listed in this guide rose to the top of the pile. The carved turn is making a comeback, and this year’s top carving skis have met the moment. A good carving ski initiates a turn, holds it like a cornering sports car, and releases into the next turn. These are directional skis, designed to be skied forward and driven down the fall line. Versatility off-piste is not this category’s jam. It’s all about the turn—your turn. Traditionally, we’ve thought of carving skis as skinny skis with 60-millimeter waist widths. But these days, carving skis come in all shapes and sizes. Those 68-millimeter, dumbed-down World Cup skis still exist, and they’re excellent carvers—but they’re not exactly approachable to the masses. So for this season, we focused our testing on the carving skis that better serve the everyday skier, not just the ex-racers: skis with wider waists and more tip rise to make them friendlier and easier to turn, but no less capable of slicing and dicing up groomers. When SKI’s testers clicked into the bindings of this season’s fleet of carvers in Deer Valley, Utah—a resort renowned for its perfectly manicured runs—they carved up a storm to determine how each ski performed on groomed terrain. When judging the best carving skis, we prioritize hard-snow integrity, carving, and stability at speed, and the seven winners excelled in these areas while nailing performance characteristics across all categories. If you haven’t tried a carving ski, there’s never been a better time to join the movement. And if you’re a tried-and-true carver, this season you’re in for quite a ride: the best carving skis of 2027 are more approachable and exciting than ever. Of the 26 carving skiss we tested at our annual SKI Test in Deer Valley, Utah, these seven stood out as top performers. They earned the highest marks across nine scoring criteria, with especially strong results in carving, hard-snow performance, and stability at speed—the three performance characteristics we prioritize when reviewing carving skis. Read more about our testing process here. Lengths: 163, 168, 173, 178, 183 cm
Dimensions: 123-80-112 mm Pros and Cons
+ Easy to lay over
+ Dependable and trustworthy at speed
– Expensive
– Unforgiving for less aggressive skiers Think of the “A” in the Montero AX as a letter grade, because this Stöckli received summa cum laude honors at our test in Deer Valley, Utah. As “Best in Test,” the Montero AX earned the highest marks in the carving category for hard-snow integrity and stability at speed, proving why this carryforward model is a perennial favorite. “Amazing edge hold and acceleration out of the turn,” said Jon Sexauer, a Colorado-based expert tester. “It’s a strong carving ski that lets advanced and expert skiers arc turns of all shapes and sizes in any snow condition.” Perhaps “all-mountain carver” best captures the Montero AX’s priorities. The visible S-shaped notches in the aluminum over the tip and tail help make turn initiation easier, while full edge contact and camber underfoot let expert skiers lay over and arc turns at cruising speeds. True, the Montero AX is more maneuverable than some Stöckli models, but less aggressive skiers may still find the strong build unforgiving. “It’s a stellar choice for those who can bend a ski but don’t want a gnarly, stiff race ski,” said Tommy Flitton, a Utah-based ski coach. “If you appreciate a smooth, approachable race-ski feel, this is amazing.” Lengths: 152, 160, 168, 176, 184 cm
Dimensions: 132-84-120 mm Pros and Cons
+ Snappy and fun all-mountain carver
+ Approachable for intermediates
– Unforgiving if you get in the backseat
– Tight turn radius resists long turns With the snappiness of Indiana Jones’ whip, the Rossignol Arcade 84 can accurately arc up corduroy or carve through cut-up snow. High scores for carving, quickness, hard-snow integrity and responsiveness won the Arcade 84 the “Most Versatile” award at our test in Deer Valley for its amazing blend of skills. “This Rossi ate up groomers, held a sharp edge on firm snow, and absolutely trenched in soft snow,” said Jon Sexauer, a Colorado-based tester. With a slightly wider waist than other skis in this category, the Arcade 84 balances high-performance precision with all-mountain approachability. A game-on construction—with a full layer of Titanal and a central power rail running down the wood core—is tamed by a curvy sidecut and voluminous, rockered tip. Testers were impressed with the easy turn initiation, as well as its ability to access high edge angles. Though quick and snappy in short turns, long turns take more effort, testers observed. And if you get in the backseat, you might get whipped. But if you can tip the Arcade 84 over and drive it down the fall line, you’re in for an adventure. Lengths: 161, 168, 175, 182 cm
Dimensions: 126-76-109 mm Pros and Cons
+ Terrific stability at speed and long-radius turns
+ Super snappy and reactive
– Lacks forgiveness in variable conditions
– One-trick pony So intuitive is the Fischer The Curv Noize GTX that testers called it a mind reader. It initiates turns seamlessly at the merest touch of pressure, earning it the highest scores in the test for carving ability. “All it wants to do is lay over on edge and absolutely trench,” said Jon Sexauer, a Colorado-based tester. “It feels so supportive and stable that you have unlimited confidence to drive it hot lap after hot lap.” Best for strong intermediates through experts, the Curv Noize GTX has a metal-and-wood core construction with Noize Control Tech—3D-printed particles placed along the length of the ski to help absorb vibrations and “quiet” it. A carbon-fiber wrap adds torsional stiffness and responsiveness. The result? “It makes groomers entertaining,” said Alex Cernichiari, a 5-foot-10 expert skier. “It can bring you out of a turn and into the next one at slow to moderate speeds, but at higher speeds, it can hold an edge perfectly.” Though versatile in turn shape and speed preference, the 76-millimeter-waisted ski does have a one-track mind and a groomer zip code: “Carve, carve, carve is all it thinks about,” quipped Todd Casey, a Colorado-based ski instructor. Testers gave it low marks in forgiveness and playfulness, citing its reluctance to do anything else. But if arcing up groomers is your idea of a great time, the Curv Noize GTX doesn’t disappoint. Lengths: 156, 163, 170, 177 cm
Dimensions: 125-76-109 mm Pros and Cons
+ Nimble, agile and approachable
+ A blast to make turns on
– Light construction means less reliable at speed
– So turny it can be fatiguing As the TikTok dancer of skis, the Salomon Addikt 76 has great moves. Case in point: it earned top scores in quickness, responsiveness and playfulness. “It’s a total hero ski,” said Avery Pesce, a Utah-based expert tester. “Not only does it have super easy turn initiation and stability at high speed, but it provides insane rebound energy out of the turn.” Like sequined pants, Salomon’s Motion Tail Technology catches the eye. The cutout in the swallowtail is designed to increase tail flexibility and turn release. Polymer pads in the metal layer add liveliness, while the shapely sidecut invites responsiveness and snap out of the turn. You don’t have to be a pro to access the Addikt 76’s talents: testers recommend this approachable ski for experts down to timid intermediates, since it can pivot and make short-to-medium-sized turns, as long as the emphasis is on “turn.” “It can get a bit fatiguing if you’re making that many energetic turns on bigger, longer runs,” said Lauren Engle, a 5-foot-4 expert skier. “But for skiers in the East and Midwest, where runs are shorter and narrower, this ski can make those conditions a blast.” Some testers noted that the swallowtail and lighter construction reduced reliability on very firm snow at speed. Icy runs aside, if workout skiing is your jam, and your ski studio has grippable groomers, the Addikt 76 will make a great partner. Lengths: 165, 170, 175, 180 cm
Dimensions: 131-82-112 mm Pros and Cons
+ Approachable and confidence inspiring
+ Very responsive and locks in on long radius turns
– Lacks some stability at high speed
– Sluggish to transition between short and long turns If the Blizzard lineup were beer styles, the Firebird would be the high-octane IPA, and the Stormbird 82 DTI would be the lager—medium-bodied, low-octane, and more popular among the masses. It’s not a watered-down race ski, but it has race-like characteristics with a flex profile that makes it more approachable for non-racers. Testers were impressed with how the Stormbird 82 DTI inspired confidence on the groomed slopes of Deer Valley, scoring it high marks across all criteria, most notably quickness, carving, and responsiveness. Though capable of making short-radius turns, the Stormbird 82 DTI is happiest skiing wide-open runs, locking into long turns on firm snow with strong tip-to-tail edge hold. This iron edge grip can also make the 82-millimeter-waisted ski feel sluggish transitioning between long and short turns, but according to testers, it just requires patience. The Stormbird 82 DTI (with dual Titanal layers) has a race-heritage construction, but the flex profile is the secret sauce. With a stiffer flex in the center, medium flex around the binding, and softer flex in the tip and tail, “you don’t feel like you’re working to bend the ski every turn, but you have energy and engagement at a moment’s notice,” said Otto Gibbons, a Washington-based ski buyer. “That nimbleness and softness makes it approachable for a huge range of skiers.” Lengths: 153, 160, 167, 174, 181 cm
Dimensions: 127-75-110.5 mm Pros and Cons
+ Good balance of energy and stability
+ Grips and rips like a GS carving ski
– Can be stiff underfoot for less aggressive skiers
– Bouncy at the tip at speed Atomic’s new Redster Q collection showcases World Cup technology paired with components that level the playing field for non-racers. As a new addition to the family, the Redster Q9 Revoshock S widens that field even further. As tester Jon Sexauer, a Colorado-based expert skier, described it, “This is a no-nonsense carver for any turn shape that can be pushed by aggressive skiers, but still remains approachable for less aggressive skiers developing their technique.” At 75 millimeters underfoot, it’s no shock that testers awarded the Redster Q9 Revoshock S high marks for hard-snow integrity, describing it as “a BFF for crushing corduroy.” Beyond groomers, testers were impressed by its ability to steer and skid easily between different snow conditions without a lot of rattle. This stability comes from the built-in stainless-steel suspension system called Revoshock S—the same technology that smooths out gnarly race-course ruts. There’s also a Carbon Boost inserted behind the heel, providing power and acceleration out of the turn, resulting in “a nice balance of energy and stability,” according to Nick Loomans, a 6-foot expert skier. “It’s like a GS carving ski that’s versatile and nimble enough to perform other types of turns, too.” Less aggressive skiers should look to the Redster Q7, built with carbon Revoshock instead of steel, because testers found the Q9 Revoshock S rather stiff underfoot. But for go-getters, the Q9 is the carver you can attack the fall line with. Lengths: 146, 152, 160, 168, 176 cm
Dimensions: 132-84-120 mm Pros and Cons
+ Initiates turns easily
+ Fun and easy to maneuver
– Has a power limit if overloaded
– Rebound energy can be off-putting Whether you’re an intermediate working on perfecting your carved turn or an instructor working on your exam maneuvers, the Rossignol Arcade W 84 is a frontside-adjacent carving ski with exceptional maneuverability. That’s the point of this 84-millimeter-waisted ski: to blend approachability with high-performance, a recipe that impressed testers across all scoring criteria, particularly in carving and quickness. “There’s not a resort skier out there on either coast that wouldn’t have fun on this ski,” said Avery Pesce, VP of merchandising at Boston Ski and Tennis. “It has so much lively energy for short turns on the side of the trail and great smoothness and stability in longer radius turns on hardpack.” The Arcade W 84 has a full-on wood and metal construction, complete with a central power rail running down the center. Add in the extended sidecut, big rockered tip and vibration absorption—a throughline from the Temptation to the Arcade line—and you get a dynamic ski that loves to arc quick turns. If you prefer a damper ski without a lot or rebound energy, look elsewhere. “The edge-to edge energy can be a lot if you’re not used to pop into the next turn,” noted Courtney Harkins, a 5-foot-8 expert skier. “Overload them too much and their incredible energy will slingshot you across the hill.” But harness the Arcade W 84’s energy, and this people-pleasing ski will oblige. The following carving skis are models that excel in specific areas like playfulness or forgiveness, offering strong alternatives for skiers with specific performance preferences. Lengths: 162, 167, 172, 177, 182 cm
Dimensions: 126-80-109 mm Pros and Cons
+ Smooth and stable
+ Reliable edge grip
– Tail can be sluggish to release
– Not as lively as some The Völkl Peregrine 80 impressed our testers with its silky-smooth feel, turn-shape versatility and edge hold, ranking it among the best in stability and hard-snow integrity. An effort to reduce weight made it more approachable, according to testers, without giving up much in return. “A Völkl with less weight? Sign me up!” quipped Otto Gibbons, hardgoods supervisor for Sturtevants Ski Mart. “The ski is grippy and can make a plethora of turn shapes, plus less weight in the tail is helpful for making it through the day.” The Peregrine 80’s 3D Radius Sidecut, which blends a tight turn radius underfoot with a longer radius at the rockered tip and tail, makes for a race-meets-freeride feel. At slow speeds, testers noted the tail takes work to release. “It’s not the liveliest at the exit of the turn,” said Jon Sexauer, a 5-foot-7 expert skier. “But put the work in, and the ski really engages and carves well.” Lengths: 145, 152, 159, 166 cm
Dimensions: 125-75-109 mm Pros and Cons
+ Good combo of dampness and responsiveness
+ Transitions well between short and long turns
– Chatters underfoot in firm conditions
– Only offered in four sizes, up to 166 cm Multitasking comes naturally to some, and that includes the Atomic Cloud Q14 Revoshock S, which moves seamlessly between long and short turns. Deemed an all-mountain carver by testers, the 75-millimeter-waisted ski favors East and West Coast skiers alike who like to mix things up. “It’s a balanced beauty,” said Marina Knight, a 5-foot-5 expert skier. “It can both smear easy turns and make higher-tempo carves for those channeling their inner Mikaela Shiffrin.” In fact, the Cloud Q14 Revoshock S uses the same stainless-steel, vibration-eating technology that’s straight from Shiffrin’s race skis. Though this groomer ski has great turn-shape versatility, testers gave it lower scores for forgiveness, detecting chatter underfoot when conditions got firmer and faster. The Cloud Q14 Revoshock S comes in only four lengths, but according to Lauren Engle, a 5-foot-4 hardgoods buyer, you can size down. “Even in a 159-centimeter length, typically short for me, this ski felt totally solid.” Lengths: 156, 163, 170, 177, 184 cm
Dimensions: 128-78-112 mm Pros and Cons
+ Very stable at speed
+ Holds a consistent edge on any pitch
– Very damp
– Hooky, sluggish skidding a turn The Porsche Macan of the group, the Head Supershape e-Rally struck testers as a smooth yet agile SUV. With Head’s directive to “bring race to piste,” the Supershape e-Rally rivaled our “Best in Test” ski for the highest score in stability at speed, with hard-snow integrity a close second. “It’s a dependable ride and a ripping groomer ski that handles any turn radius you ask of it,” said Tommy Flitton, a Utah-based ski coach. With a World Cup Sandwich Cap construction that includes wood, graphene, Titanal and carbon, the e-Rally channels a Master’s race-ski vibe, with a GS turn radius and strong edge hold. Just don’t expect a playful, quick turner: according to testers, the one-track-mind, directional e-Rally is damp and feels sluggish in a skidded turn. But for intermediates through experts who prioritize dependability and edge hold over rebound energy, this ski will deliver consistent performance on any pitch. See how the best carving skis of 2027 stack up in SKI’s individual scoring criteria. Carving skis are the narrow-waisted skis designed for on-piste skiing. Carving skis typically feature waist widths below 85 millimeters. With more exaggerated side cuts (hourglass shape) than you’ll find on wider skis, carving skis are designed to chew up corduroy and hardpack snow as well as make short radius slalom turns or long arcing GS turns. It used to be that only the best skiers could handle the race-inspired skis available in the narrowest of waist widths. These stiff and demanding carving skis tended to be unapproachable to intermediates and advanced skiers looking to improve their technique. But that’s no longer the case. Featuring more tip rocker, wider shovels, and lighterweight construction materials than carving skis of the past, many models now allow strong intermediates to experience the locked-in feeling and power of these narrow-waisted skis. Our top carving ski of 2027 is the Stöckli Montero AX. It outperformed all the other carving skis we tested in Deer Valley, Utah. Testers raved about its carving ability on groomed terrain, its precision on edge, and its smooth feeling underfoot. For 2027, our testers named the Rossignol Arcade W 84 the best carving ski for women. Our female testers appreciated its precision, dependability, and carving abilities. Carving skis give it away in the name: they’re built to arc carved turns on groomed terrain. Think race skis, but made more accessible to the everyday skier. Frontside skis can be just as reliable on groomers and hardpack, even with a little added tip rocker. But because frontside skis are typically a little straighter from tip to tail with a slightly wider waist, they don’t have the same innate carving capabilities as carving skis. Where frontside skis win out is in the versatility department—they’re designed to perform even off the groomers. In short: Carving skis are the scalpels of skis, designed to be handled by an experienced hand and leave precise incisions on the snow. A frontside ski is more like a machete—it’s still sharp and effective but doesn’t require you to be as precise in your cutting. In truth, most skis are unisex and not gender-specific. Many brands produce the ski with the exact same construction technologies for both genders, but often create two different top sheets/graphics to appeal to men vs. women. In general, men and women can use the same ski but may want to choose different lengths depending on their height, weight, and their skiing style/ability. A handful of brands design true women’s skis with construction tweaks for female physiology. These skis generally come in shorter lengths (from 170 cm down to 150 cm) and use slightly softer, lighter construction materials. As a general rule of thumb, the shorter the ski, the easier it is to turn and control. So if you’re a beginner, reach for a ski that’s about chin-height. More advanced skiers often choose skis that are as long as they are tall, since longer skis provide more stability at speed and float in deep snow. So the best ski length for you will depend on your height, your skill level, and what type of skiing you hope to do. A ski-shop employee can help point you in the right direction. Note that ski length is relative. Narrow carving skis tend to ski longer than their length because they feature more effective edge, while powder skis tend to ski shorter than their length because they feature more rocker in the tip and tail. Dozens of this year's carving test skis lined up at the rack, ready for testers to grab their next pair at the 2026 SKI Test.Re Wikstrom Each year, SKI’s editorial team conducts one of the most rigorous and trusted all-mountain ski tests in the industry. At the 2026 SKI Test in Deer Valley, Utah, 18 experienced skiers from across the country tested 26 carving skis in real-world resort conditions. To reduce subjectivity, all testers skied each model on the same day, in the same conditions, and submitted digital scorecards evaluating each ski across nine criteria: When judging the best carving skis, we place the greatest emphasis on hard-snow integrity, carving, and responsiveness—three key indicators of a top-tier carving ski. The seven winners on this list earned consistently high marks across all categories, especially those three. The skis included in the “More Skis We Recommend” section are models that excel in specific areas like playfulness or forgiveness, offering strong alternatives for skiers with specific performance preferences. Learn more about our testing methodology and scoring criteria here. Our ski reviews are the result of the largest, most rigorous on-snow test in the industry. We never charge brands to participate and don’t guarantee coverage—our annual SKI Test is a fully independent editorial project designed to deliver objective, in-depth reviews. Our expert testers include ski instructors, ski patrollers, ski shop owners, hardgoods buyers, ski technicians, and race and freeride coaches. We handpick this crew for their professional expertise and intentionally include a range of body types, ages, and home mountains to reflect the broader ski community. Bottom line: There’s no pay-to-play here—just honest feedback from people who know skis. Meet some of our veteran testers below: Crabtree spent every winter weekend brown-bagging lunch and skiing bell to bell in New Hampshire and ski racing around New England’s storied race hills. After a stint on the Bates College alpine ski team, she headed west to coach at Ski Club Vail, and then moved to the mountains above Boulder to get her Masters at the University of Colorado. An internship at SKI lead to eight years as an editor and director of the women’s ski test. She has been testing and writing about skis, boots, and gear since 1999. Born and raised in Salt Lake City, Flitton joined the Snowbird ski team as a young racer at the age of 7. He worked his way through the ranks as a racer, spending time at a ski academy in Vermont before returning to his favorite mountain in Utah. Now he spends his time coaching young freeriders how to send it big at Snowbird. He’s a veteran gear tester who has tested skis for SKI, Outside, and Powder. Loomans grew up in Mukwonago, Wisc., and took up skiing at Alpine Valley Resort. He was an USCSA All-American skier for the University of Minnesota. Translation: He knows how to bend a ski.

title: GS holds 5th hackathon as chairman says AI is transforming workplace safety - 헤럴드경제
content: GS Group held its 5th GS Group Hackathon on Monday at the Westin Seoul Parnas in Gangnam-gu, Seoul. The hackathon brings together GS employees to propose ideas using AI, from in-house productivity improvements to broader business innovations. A total of 923 people are expected to participate through Tuesday — 797 employees from GS affiliates and 126 external participants — making it the largest edition to date. Cumulative participation over the past five years has reached 2,732. This year's theme is "Play with Gen AI Season 3: Build and Act," reflecting a dual focus on creating AI-powered outputs that actually work (Build) and connecting them to real workplaces and business operations (Act). GS Group Chairman Heo Tae-soo, who attended the event, said ideas from employees who know the workplace best, combined with AI, had become a force for changing how industrial safety is managed. "I will actively support the challenges that began at the hackathon so they can take root beyond GS, reach more workplaces and lead to new value," he said. GS Caltex Vice Chairman and CEO Heo Se-hong, who delivered the opening remarks, said the hackathon was a place to bring out and act on ideas that are rarely tried in everyday work. "I hope you spend the next two days asking questions freely, taking on challenges and discovering new possibilities," he said. This year's participants are working with AI-ready data. Applying AI to industrial settings requires data to be organized in a format that AI can read — a step that must come first. Even when data has accumulated on-site, inconsistent formats and standards make retrieving and processing it time-consuming. To ease this bottleneck, GS has been refining and structuring data gathered across various business sites, including power plants and convenience stores. Its innovation unit 52g, for example, has organized tacit knowledge from GS Donghae Power — covering operations, maintenance and facilities — into AI-readable form, and is developing a power-plant-specific AI model that understands on-site knowledge and work procedures. At this hackathon, participants are combining AI-ready data with GS's AI transformation platform MISO to solve real workplace problems. The key is cutting the time spent on data preparation so ideas can be implemented faster and deployed on-site sooner. Kim Jin-a, a GS executive director who helped organize the hackathon, said five years of the event had established GS's field-centered AI transformation as an innovation model that drives real change, beyond slogans or one-off experiments. "We plan to support this year's outputs through verification and refinement so they translate into tangible results in actual work and business performance," she said. Meanwhile, the safety management AI agent team AIR (AI Risk Assessment) received the Open Innovation Award at the event. AIR originated from an idea proposed at the 3rd GS Group Hackathon by five employees from GS Power's safety and mechanical divisions. Users enter a task name and a brief description, and the AI automatically identifies potential hazards, assigns risk ratings and suggests preventive safety measures. Built by frontline workers rather than professional developers using MISO, it is now in use at more than 330 worksites, including small and midsize businesses.

title: Mailbag: Fans React After Vikings Hold Bears Scoreless on 9 Consecutive Possessions in 9-3 Win - Minnesota Vikings
content: Do you have a comment or question? Send it to the Mailbag. Every Monday we'll post several comments and/or questions. Click here to submit a comment or question to Mailbag. Remember to include your name and town in the email. If Twitter / X is your jam, you can send a question to me that way as well. The Vikings have started 2-0 with both wins coming against division foes for the first time since 2003 and third time ever. Minnesota's defense bowed up at the critical moments, denying Chicago points on all but one drive (the first of the game for the Bears) and held on for a 9-3 win in the lowest-scoring game in series history. The Bears put together a 13-play drive that gained 51 yards before a string of penalties forced a punt. An 11-play, 64-yarder to open the second half ended when Jalen Redmond forced a fumble recovered by Isaiah Rodgers at the Minnesota 1. A 12-play, 62-yarder ended with Rodgers blocking a 23-yard field goal, and an eight-play drive covered 44 yards but ended at the Minnesota 12 on the game's final snap, which was hiked with one second remaining. The offense leaned on getting points on the opening drive by taking an early chance — a 30-yard pass from Carson Wentz to Justin Jefferson that moved the receiver past Randy Moss for second on Minnesota's all-time catches leaderboard — and leaned on the reliability and ruggedness of Aaron Jones, Sr., who improved to 16-2 in 18 career games against the Bears. Will Reichard was good on field goals of 35, 49 and 39 yards, despite some soggy socks and shoes. View game action photos from the Vikings Week 2 game vs. the Bears at Soldier Field. What a great defensive battle this game was. The ending was just insane. So sorry to see Caleb Williams go down on that non-contact injury. I was just amazed at the fourth quarter blocked FG and subsequent drive — earning a rare fourth up! Below are my four ups and three downs for the game: 1. Vikings defense forcing Caleb to make a poor first quarter throw on third-and-long resulting in a Vikings interception. Nicely done! 2. Outstanding defensive play heading into the end of the half. We forced a punt and after our offense stalled and we punted, we stopped their final drive as well. 3. Redmond's punch-out fumble by the Vikings defense on the Bears 1-yard line.  Excellent play. 4. The fourth quarter blocked FG and, just as important, the almost game-sealing drive where we ran the ball and milked the clock. Only to have the defense save the day with no time on the clock. Wow. 1. Third-and-2 for Vikings. Ends up with play clock running out and snap over Wentz's head. Unacceptable on both fronts. 2. At the end of the half we had to punt. Great punt and weak and ineffective punt coverage when it mattered most. We set the conditions for Caleb to tie the game or take the lead by allowing that return. Our punt coverage team should be thanking our defense for their second 2-minute stop. 3. Overall offensive production was too weak. But I will take that fourth quarter drive any time! I obviously never want any player to go through an injury, regardless of what team he plays for and wish Williams well in his recovery. Injuries are part of the game, and the Vikings have gone through many over the years. Prior to Williams' injury, it seemed like the Vikings designed and executed a great game plan that constrained a team that scored 59 points at Carolina in Week 1. Having covered teams that have fallen victim to the "Peanut Punch" copyrighted by Charles Tillman, it was impressive to see Redmond's wallop with Tillman in attendance. Rodgers grazed Cairo Santos' field goal at the end of Chicago's first possession and brought an even better one on his next try, keeping it a 6-3 game with 6:21 remaining. There seemed to be a bit of disarray prior to the snap. Perhaps a timeout would have been in order. It was super critical that Wentz hustled to recover the ball. title: GS Engineering & Construction holds AI competition finals, eyes real-world deployment - 헤럴드경제
content: Over 90 teams competed; 700-plus employees trained and coached Top prize goes to AI solution for reviewing plant steel shop drawings GS Engineering & Construction is accelerating its digital transformation by moving beyond company-wide AI training to deploying employee-developed AI solutions in actual construction work. The company announced Monday that it had selected 12 projects with strong real-world applicability through its in-house AI competition, AX Recipe, and held the finals Friday. At the finals, 12 teams demonstrated AI solutions they had developed themselves. Voting by management, including CEO Heo Yun-hong, and employees determined the top three teams. This year's top prize went to an AI solution for streamlining the review of plant steel shop drawings. The winning entry replaced a manual process of visually cross-checking thousands of steel members one by one with an AI-based solution, cutting review time by more than 80 percent and significantly improving accuracy. The representative of the winning team will receive an invitation to attend CES 2027, the world's largest consumer electronics and IT trade show. Now in its second year, AX Recipe — launched last year — is GS Engineering & Construction's flagship innovation program in which employees use AI to solve real workplace problems. This year the format shifted from individual to team participation, yielding a broad range of practical AI solutions ready for immediate deployment across the company's business lines, including architecture, infrastructure and plant construction, going well beyond simple task automation. More than 90 teams entered the competition, and some 700 employees received AI training and dedicated coaching over July and August. The finals showcased a variety of construction-specific ideas, including a defect-prevention platform integration solution for the design and construction phases, a project contract change tracking system, and a solution for cross-checking 3D design models against specifications. GS Engineering & Construction plans to review the top projects for broader rollout across divisions and the company before applying them to operations in stages. "Through AX Recipe, we confirmed that our employees can go beyond learning about AI to actually applying it on the job and delivering tangible results," a company official said. "We will continue to strengthen a system that organically connects training, hands-on practice and real-world application, and we will keep expanding a data and AI utilization model tailored to the construction industry." Meanwhile, GS Engineering & Construction posted operating profit of 232.4 billion won ($168 million) in the first half of this year, up 41.8 percent from 164.2 billion won in the same period last year.
